cues.text: Voice for a Silent Bishop

Vincent , born at Huesca in Roman Spain, was ordained deacon under Bishop Valerius of Saragossa , who suffered from a speech impediment and so entrusted Vincent with the preaching duties of the diocese.
Vincent proved so effective a preacher that, in the Catholic Encyclopedia's words, he brought about the conversion of a considerable number of sinners and pagans through his sermons alone.
Arrest Under Dacian

When the persecution of Diocletian reached Spain, the provincial governor Dacian had both Vincent and Bishop Valerius arrested and dragged in chains to Valencia , where they were held in prison for a long period.
Valerius was eventually sentenced only to exile, but Dacian then subjected Vincent alone to escalating and prolonged torture.
Torments Endured
According to his traditional Acts, preserved in traditional accounts, Vincent was stretched on the rack and torn with iron hooks.
The Spanish Christian poet Prudentius poetically commemorated these Acts about a century after Vincent’s death.
Vincent was then roasted on a gridiron and thrown into a cell whose floor was strewn with broken pottery shards.
Vincent is remembered as having told his tormentors, with striking composure, that they would tire of inflicting torment long before he tired of enduring it.
A Refusal to the End
When his jailers offered him a final chance at release in exchange for surrendering the sacred Scriptures to be burned, Vincent refused outright.
He equally refused an offer of a soft, comfortable bed intended to tempt his resolve into surrender—a comfort in which, tradition holds, he instead peacefully expired.
His spirit had outlasted every attempt to break it by force or by ease.
The Raven and the Sea
Popular legend surrounding his death adds that his body, left exposed to be devoured by vultures, was instead protected by a raven.
The raven drove the carrion birds away, and when the governor had his remains cast into the sea to prevent Christian veneration, the body washed ashore.
It was recovered and buried by a devout widow.
Legacy

St. Augustine himself preached four separate sermons in Vincent's honor, testifying that his fame had already spread, in Augustine's words, 'throughout the Roman empire and wherever you find the name Christian.'
Ranked with Stephen and Lawrence among the Church's three most celebrated early deacon-martyrs, Vincent remains the patron of Valencia, Lisbon, and Saragossa.
Devotion to him, spreading rapidly across Spain, France, and England, made him one of the most widely venerated martyrs of the entire early Western Church.
